units.text: Five trustees guard one vault. It opens only when its dial is turned to one mark, the secret, and a wrong mark sets off the alarm. To anyone outside, the secret could be any of the eleven marks. This strip shows which marks are still possible for whoever we're watching.

The simplest plan is to tell one trustee. But then one accident or one lost note can shut the vault for good, and one bribe can open it for the wrong person. So give all five a copy. One absence no longer locks the vault, but now each trustee can open it alone, and any one can let it slip.

What the trustees want lies in between. Any three of them together should be able to work out the secret from what they hold, and any two should learn nothing about it. That number, three, is called the threshold.

From here on, opening the vault means working out the secret from what the trustees were handed, not guessing it. With a threshold of three, two trustees can be away and the vault still opens. Before any mathematics, how would you hand out the secret to make that work?

Whatever a trustee is handed, call it their share. The first idea most people have is to make each share a piece of the secret. Try the smallest case, a vault that needs both of two trustees, A and B. Cut the secret into two ordinary numbers that add up to it, two for A and three for B.
Together they add two and three, get five, and the door opens. But what does B's three say about the secret on its own?

Quite a lot. A's piece can't be less than zero, so the secret is at least three. Zero, one and two are crossed off, and only eight possible secrets are left. And the bigger the piece, the more it gives away. A piece of the secret is part of the secret.

Cut pieces fail a second way too. They only work all together, so with A away, B's three still leaves eight possible secrets, and the vault stays shut. So cutting the secret up leaks, and it needs every piece. The leak gets fixed first, and the fix is the dial itself.

Adding on the dial means turning. From nine, turn seven marks forward, past ten and round through zero, and you stop at five. So on this dial, nine plus seven is five. Ten plus one is zero. Taking away means turning back, so five take away seven is nine.

Now share the secret on the dial instead. The dealer, who knows the secret, spins a spare dial fairly and gives A wherever it stops, nine. B gets the turn from nine to the secret, seven. Together they turn nine on by seven, reach five, and the door opens. What does B's seven say about the secret now?
Nothing at all. If A had zero, the secret would be seven. If A had one, eight. Go through all eleven marks A could hold, and you meet all eleven secrets, once each.
A's mark came from a fair spin, so B's seven fits every secret equally well. A circle has no floor and no ceiling, so a share can't push the secret above or below anything.
That fixes the leak, but this vault still needs both trustees.

Back to five trustees and a threshold of three. Here is where we're headed. Using the secret and two fair spins, the dealer hands out five shares, eight, three, one, two and six. Trustees one, two and three bring their eight, three and one, work out the secret, five, and the door opens. How they do it comes later.

Trustees four and five hold two and six. Like anyone, they can pick a mark at random. They'd be right one time in eleven, and the other ten times the alarm goes off. So the demand isn't that two trustees can never get lucky. It's that their two shares tell them nothing, not one mark ruled out, not even a hint that the secret is odd.
Is that even possible? Could two shares be completely useless, when three open the vault?

Here's an experiment. Feed the dealer's method every secret from zero to ten, with every one of the hundred and twenty-one ways its two spins could land. For each secret, count the ways of spinning that hand trustees four and five exactly what they hold, a two and a six. Will some secrets fit more ways than others?
No. Every secret fits exactly one way, and a different way each time. So the pair's two and six fit every secret equally well.
They can still guess, but their shares can't tell them what to guess. With fair spins, every secret is exactly as likely as it was before they met.
Two shares can't determine the secret, and three can. The rest of the story is why both are true.

There is an older way to get any three of five, with padlocks. Put ten padlocks on the door, one for each pair of trustees. Each padlock's key goes to everyone outside its pair. The lock for four and five has its keys with one, two and three. Every trustee then carries six keys. Any three trustees together hold a key to every lock, because no pair contains all three of them.
How many locks stop trustees four and five?
Just one, their own. And no lock can do that job for two different pairs, or it would also stop the three or four trustees in those pairs together. So ten locks is the fewest that works.

Adi Shamir's nineteen seventy-nine paper, How to Share a Secret, opens with a bigger version, taken from an older book. Any six of eleven scientists must be able to open a cabinet, and no five can. The smallest answer is four hundred and sixty-two locks, with two hundred and fifty-two keys for each scientist.
Shamir's own answer is the dealer's method, with no locks at all. Each trustee carries one number from the same dial as the secret.

To see the dealer's method, start with a simpler rule, any two of five. Mark the secret as a point at position zero, height five. The dealer spins once, and say it gives four. Draw the straight line that starts at the secret and climbs four for every step to the right.

Trustee one sits at position one, trustee two at position two, and so on. Each trustee's share is the line's height at their own position. Nine, thirteen, seventeen, twenty-one and twenty-five. Any two trustees can lay down their two points and redraw the line, and the line tells them the height at zero.
One point is not enough to redraw it, but on ordinary paper it still gives something away. Trustee five holds twenty-five. Which secrets could go with that?
Just three, zero, five or ten. No other secret is twenty-five take away five times a spin.
Ordinary numbers keep growing, and their size leaks, just as B's piece did. So wrap the heights around the dial instead.
Nine stays nine. Thirteen goes once round the dial and lands on two. Seventeen lands on six, twenty-one on ten, and twenty-five on three.

On the dial the points look scattered, but the rule is the same. Start at the secret and turn on four for each step. Take trustees two and three, holding two and six. They are one step apart and differ by four, so each step adds four. Step back twice from trustee two. Two take away four is nine, and nine take away four is five, the secret.
Now trustee two is alone, holding two, which is the secret plus twice the spin. If the spin could be any of the eleven marks, how many secrets fit that share?

All eleven, one for each spin. Spin zero means the secret is two. Spin one means two take away two, zero. Doubling is the reason. On this dial, the doubles of zero to ten are zero, two, four, six, eight, ten, then one, three, five, seven and nine. Every mark, once.
So each spin gives its own secret, and trustee two's share fits every secret equally well, just like B's seven.

For any three of five, replace the line with a curve. The dealer spins twice, and say the dial gives seven, then seven again. Every trustee's height is the secret, plus seven times their position, plus seven times their position squared. Trustee one gets five plus seven plus seven, nineteen. Trustee two gets five plus fourteen plus twenty-eight, forty-seven.

Three, four and five get eighty-nine, a hundred and forty-five, and two hundred and fifteen. On paper, these points lie on one smooth curve, a parabola, and any three of them pin it down. Now wrap them. Where does trustee two's forty-seven land on the dial?
Forty-seven is four elevens and three more, so it lands on three. All five shares come out eight, three, one, two and six, the very shares from the vault.
A rule like this, the secret plus spins times powers of the position, is called a polynomial. One spin gives a line, for any two. Two spins give a curve, for any three.

Back to trustees four and five, with their two and six, and the experiment from before. Now we can see what it found. Through their two points and the secret five runs the dealer's curve, with spins seven and seven. How many curves of this kind run through their two points and the secret zero instead?

Exactly one, with spins one and four. Check it: trustee four's height would be sixty-eight, which lands on two, and trustee five's a hundred and five, which lands on six. For the secret one, the spins would be zero and nine. Every secret gets its own curve and its own pair of spins. Here are all eleven. Each one is a dealing the dealer could have made, if the secret had been different.

And the hundred and twenty-one spin pairs are all equally likely. Whatever the secret, exactly one of them hands trustees four and five a two and a six. So what they hold is just as likely under every secret, and meeting has taught them nothing.

Notice what that argument used. On paper, a curve also runs through any secret and the same two points, so the picture alone can't be the reason. On paper, their heights are a hundred and forty-five and two hundred and fifteen. For the secret zero, the curve through them needs spins of nine and a quarter and six and three quarters, and no spin can be that. Only the secret five gets whole spins, so on paper their heights give the secret away.

On the dial, every one of the eleven curves comes from real spins, one pair each, all equally likely. That count is the proof, and the pictures only help us see it. Now let trustee one join them, holding eight. How many of the eleven curves pass through eight at position one?
Just one. Each curve passes position one at a different mark, and only the curve for five passes at eight. The strip drops from eleven secrets to one.
The same count holds for every pair of trustees and every two shares they could hold. Two shares leave all eleven secrets, and any third share leaves exactly one.

Why does the dial have eleven marks? We count in tens, so ten would seem the natural choice. Deal the same secret with the same two spins, but on a ten-mark dial. Would trustees four and five still learn nothing?

On ten marks, each height simply lands on its last digit: nine, seven, nine, five and five. So trustees four and five would hold five and five, not two and six. Now run the experiment again: for each secret, count the spin pairs that would hand them those two cards. On eleven marks, two and six fitted every secret exactly one way. On ten marks, five and five come from ten spin pairs, and every one of them has the secret five. These two could work out the secret alone.

How? Write their heights out. Trustee four's is the secret, plus four of the first spin, plus sixteen of the second. Trustee five's is the secret, plus five of the first, plus twenty-five of the second. To get rid of the first spin, make both hold the same amount of it. Five copies of trustee four's height hold twenty, and so do four copies of trustee five's. Take one from the other, and the first spin cancels. What's left is the secret, minus twenty of the second spin.

On ten marks, twenty of anything lands on zero, so the second spin drops out too and leaves the secret bare. With their cards, five times five, minus four times five, is twenty-five minus twenty, which is five. On eleven marks, minus twenty lands on two instead, so the same sum is the secret plus twice the second spin. With their two and six, five times two, minus four times six, is minus fourteen, which lands on eight. Every secret makes eight with exactly one second spin, so eight fits them all.
And it isn't only this pair. On ten marks, nine of the ten pairs of trustees can always cross off some secrets, and two pairs always find it. Only trustees one and three learn nothing.

What went wrong? On ten marks, marks that aren't zero can multiply to zero. Two times five is ten, which lands on zero. Watch what that does to multiplying by five. On ten marks, five times any mark lands on zero or five and nothing else, so the ten marks crowd onto two.

That's how a single share leaks. On ten marks, the straight line from before deals nine, three, seven, one and five. Trustee five's share is the secret plus five times the spin, and five times the spin is zero or five. So that share alone leaves two possible secrets, here zero and five. Now do the same on eleven marks. Multiply every mark by five. How many different marks come out?

All eleven. One goes to five, two to ten, and three to fifteen, which wraps round to four. Each step lands five further round the dial, and every mark is reached exactly once. So on eleven marks, trustee five's share would fit every secret.

What's the difference? Ten is two times five, so two and five can each bring part of the ten, and their product lands on zero. Eleven doesn't split like that. It's prime: its only factors are one and itself. Landing on zero means being a multiple of eleven. Every whole number splits into primes in only one way, so a product of marks has eleven among its primes only if one of the marks does. No mark from one to ten does. So on eleven marks, a product lands on zero only when one of its factors is zero.

So if two marks gave the same answer after multiplying by five, five times their difference would land on zero, and that can't happen unless they're the same mark. The same holds for every multiplier from one to ten: each one only shuffles the eleven marks. On ten marks, only one, three, seven and nine do.

That's what the counting needs. Any prime number of marks works, if it's more than the number of trustees, so that each one has a position besides zero, and the secret is one of its marks. For five trustees, seven marks would already do.

Back at the start, trustees one, two and three brought their eight, three and one, and the door opened. How they did it was left for later. They know three points of the dealer's curve, but not its spins. So how can three numbers give five?

To see the idea, go back to paper, where nothing wraps, and pretend for now that they knew their heights there: nineteen, forty-seven and eighty-nine. Three points pin a parabola down, so the one through these is the dealer's curve, and its height at zero is the secret. The trick is to build that curve out of simpler pieces.

Give each trustee a helper curve. Trustee one's helper is one at position one, and zero at positions two and three. Trustee two's is one at position two, and trustee three's is one at position three, each zero at the other two positions. A helper answers to its own trustee only.

Now scale each helper by its trustee's height: nineteen times the first, forty-seven times the second, and eighty-nine times the third, and add them. At position one, the second and third helpers are zero, and zero times anything is zero, so the sum there is nineteen. At position two it's forty-seven, and at three it's eighty-nine. The sum passes through all three points. But can a helper like that be built? What simple recipe is zero at both positions two and three?

Position minus two, times position minus three. Each factor is zero at its own position, so the product is zero at both. At position one it's minus one times minus two, which is two, so halve it, and the helper is one there. On paper, halving is no trouble. The same steps make the other two. Trustee two's is position minus one, times position minus three, which is minus one at position two, so divide by minus one. Trustee three's is position minus one, times position minus two, which is two at position three, so halve it.

Each helper is made from a fixed number, a multiple of the position, and a multiple of the position squared. Adding scaled helpers keeps that form. No higher power appears just by adding. The sum passes through the dealer's three points. Only one curve of that form can do that, so the sum is the dealer's curve itself. Its height at zero is the secret.

So read each helper at position zero. Trustee one's is minus two times minus three, which is six, halved, so three. That's trustee one's weight: how much their height counts for at zero. Trustee two's is minus one times minus three, which is three, divided by minus one, so its weight is minus three. Trustee three's is minus one times minus two, which is two, halved, so one. The weights use only the positions, one, two and three, which everyone knows.

So on paper, the secret is three times nineteen, minus three times forty-seven, plus one times eighty-nine. That's fifty-seven, minus a hundred and forty-one, plus eighty-nine, which is five. But the trustees never see those heights. They hold only the wrapped numbers, eight, three and one. Will the same weights still work on what they hold?
Yes. Three times eight, minus three times three, plus one times one is sixteen, and sixteen lands on five. The dial turns to five, and the door opens, just as it did before.

Here's why. Each share is its height with whole elevens taken off. Nineteen is eight and one eleven, forty-seven is three and four elevens, and eighty-nine is one and eight elevens. Whole weights turn whole elevens into whole elevens. So the sum on paper and the sum on the cards can differ only by whole elevens, and sixteen is five and one eleven. That's why wrapping first changes nothing, as long as the weights are whole. On the dial, they're three, eight and one.

Another day, trustees two, four and five come, holding three, two and six. On paper their heights were forty-seven, a hundred and forty-five, and two hundred and fifteen. The trustees never see those heights; we use them to understand the helpers.

Trustee two's helper starts as position minus four, times position minus five. At its own position the product is six, so divide the whole helper by six to make it one there. At zero the product is twenty, so its weight is twenty divided by six: ten thirds.
Trustee four uses position minus two, times position minus five. At its own position the product is minus two; at zero it is ten. Dividing ten by minus two gives its weight, minus five.

Trustee five uses position minus two, times position minus four. At its own position the product is three; at zero it is eight. So its weight is eight thirds. The same construction works; the weights just need not be whole numbers.

On paper, ten thirds of forty-seven, minus five times a hundred and forty-five, plus eight thirds of two hundred and fifteen, is exactly five. The weighted helpers still rebuild the same curve, so their sum at zero still gives the secret.
But the trustees hold only the wrapped shares. Will these ordinary fractions still work on their cards, three, two and six?
Here they do, by luck. The ten thirds of three is ten, minus five times two is minus ten, and eight thirds of six is sixteen. The sum is sixteen again, which lands on five.

For these particular cards, three and six are multiples of three, so each fractional term happens to be whole. We have not shown that ordinary fractions work on every dealing. What happens when those thirds do not cancel?
Now deal the same secret with spins zero and one instead. On paper, the heights at our trustees are nine, twenty-one and thirty. Their wrapped cards are nine, ten and eight. Keep those cards in view.
Using the same weights, ten thirds, minus five and eight thirds, gives four thirds. Four thirds is no mark on the dial. The ordinary fraction recipe has failed.

This is not just an awkward example. For this secret, eighty of the hundred and twenty-one spin pairs leave a fractional sum. A third of an eleven is not a whole eleven, so the reason whole weights survived wrapping no longer applies.

Clear the thirds first. Three times each weight is a whole number: ten, minus fifteen and eight. On paper, multiplying every weight by three makes the sum three times the secret. Whole weights keep removed elevens whole, so this new sum survives wrapping.

Now use the cards, nine, ten and eight. The weighted terms are ninety, minus a hundred and fifty, plus sixty-four, which is four. We have recovered three times the secret on the dial, rather than the secret itself.
So three times the secret lands on four. Which mark, times three, lands on four?

Five. Three times five is fifteen, which lands on four. And no other mark does: the row of threes reaches every mark exactly once, just as the row of fives did on eleven marks. We undo times three by finding its unique starting mark.
Back to the original shares, three, two and six. Ten times three, minus fifteen times two, plus eight times six, is forty-eight. That lands on four. Undo times three and the secret is five again.
There's a shortcut for undoing times three, without searching the whole row each time. Which mark, times three, lands on one?
Four. Three times four is twelve, which lands on one. Multiplying by three and then by four therefore lands you back where you started. Together, those operations multiply by one on this dial.

Our target was four. Multiply it by four: sixteen lands on five, the secret. That's what dividing by three means here: multiplying by four. We are undoing multiplication on the dial, not cutting a mark into pieces.

Now the weights can live on the dial too. Ten thirds becomes ten times four, which is forty, landing on seven. Minus five lands on six. Eight thirds becomes eight times four, which is thirty-two, landing on ten.
Use those weights on the same cards. Seven times three, plus six times two, plus ten times six, is ninety-three. That's eight elevens and five, the secret again, now with no fractions at all.
Every mark except zero has a partner like four on eleven marks. Its row of multiples reaches one exactly once. Here are all the partners: each product lands on one.
On ten marks, two, four, five, six and eight have no partner. The shortcut needs that partner to exist. Division on a dial is a rule with a condition, not ordinary fraction arithmetic.
With partners, helpers and weights work on the dial itself. Any three of the five get the same answer. There are ten ways to pick three trustees, and all ten rebuild five.

But why must that happen? Keep trustees two and four, and try a different recipe. This trial gives them the same cards. We have not checked trustee five yet. Could a different recipe match that card too?

Subtract the original recipe from the trial. Subtract constants from constants, position terms from position terms, and squared-position terms from squared-position terms. The difference still has no power higher than squared. Wherever the cards match, the difference lands on zero.
Suppose the card at trustee five matched as well. How many distinct positions would make the difference zero?

Three. But this trial fails: at trustee five it gives nine instead of six, so the difference is three. Its only zeros are at two and four. Let's find out why a nonzero difference of this kind can never manage that extra zero.

Our difference can be written as position minus two, times position minus four. The table follows those two factors and their product around the whole dial. The product lands on zero exactly at the marks where either factor does.

That last step uses the partners we just found. If a product is zero and a nonzero factor has a partner, multiply by that partner. It undoes that factor, leaving the other factor alone. So the other factor must be zero. Two nonzero marks cannot hide each other on this dial.

Now take any difference that is zero at a mark called r. Dividing its polynomial by position minus r leaves no remainder, because the value at r is zero. What's left has at most a position term: a line. The first factor is zero only at r. A line that is not zero everywhere has at most one zero: undo its slope to find that position.

That gives at most two zeros for a difference that is not zero everywhere. If the remaining line is zero everywhere, the whole difference is zero everywhere too. So three matching positions force that exceptional case: the trial and the original are the same recipe.

The reasoning works for any three distinct trustees, not just our chosen trio. Their cards determine the whole recipe, including its value at position zero: the secret. That's why all ten groups return five. The prime dial and the distinct positions are doing essential work.

Let's return to the ten-mark dial. Keep the original recipe, but wrap its answers on ten marks. Focus on trustees one, three and five. Their cards are nine, nine and five. Can a change to the recipe hide from all of them?

Try adding the line five plus five times position. At our chosen trustees, it gives ten, twenty and thirty. Those are full turns around this dial, so each addition lands on zero. At the secret's position, the same line adds five instead.
Now add that line to the whole recipe. Will those trustees notice the change? And what does the secret become?

Nothing changes on their cards. They still hold nine, nine and five. But the secret becomes zero. The new recipe is zero plus two times position plus seven times position squared. It agrees with all their cards and opens a different secret.

This is a failure to reconstruct, not merely an inconvenient way to divide. Both recipes are allowed on this dial, and these trustees see exactly the same evidence. They cannot decide whether the secret is five or zero, however clever their calculation.

That does not mean every trio fails on ten marks. Here we check every trio of the original five trustees against every allowed recipe. Nine of the ten groups determine the secret. The group we just watched is the exception: both answers survive.

Eleven marks rule out this hiding place. There, a line that is not zero everywhere has at most one zero. Our invisible line cannot exist. The prime dial gives the guarantee for every distinct trio, which is exactly the promise that the ten-mark example breaks.

Back on our eleven-mark dial, here is the promise. Any three genuine shares recover the secret. Any two reveal no information about it. Let's return to trustees four and five, holding two and six, and see exactly what that promise needs.

The dealer must follow the recipe honestly. Both spins must be fair, independent of each other and of the secret, and kept secret. Every mark must be allowed, zero included. Being random is not enough if the spins favor some marks or depend on the secret.

Why those conditions? For each possible secret, exactly one of the one hundred twenty-one spin pairs produces these cards. That is the same chance for every secret. Seeing the cards therefore leaves the relative chances of the secrets exactly as they were before.

Now change only the dealer's rule. Refuse a second spin of zero, so the curve must really bend. The trustees know this restriction. Looking at their same cards, can they rule out a possible secret? Which one?

Eight. The unique straight line through their points is eight plus four times position. At trustee four it reaches twenty-four, which wraps to two. At trustee five it reaches twenty-eight, which wraps to six. Its second spin is zero, so this is the forbidden recipe.

There is no other recipe for secret eight that gives these cards. So with straight lines forbidden, eight is impossible. The other ten candidates still have an allowed recipe. The cards have taught the trustees something, even though they cannot yet recover the secret.

Restore the proper rule, with zero allowed. In our toy, if the secret itself is chosen uniformly from eleven marks, a blind guess succeeds one time in eleven. Two shares do not improve that chance. If some secrets were likelier beforehand, their chances stay that way instead.

For a real key, use a large space and an unpredictable secret, with proper random spins. A huge dial does not rescue an easy-to-guess password. The guarantee is precise: these shares add no information about the secret. They do not erase what somebody already knows or can guess.

The promise tells us what shares reveal. It does not promise that trustees tell the truth. Keep the honest dealer, but allow at most one false share. Trustee three now hands in two instead of one. Could the others discover the lie, and could they identify the liar?

Use the same weights, three, minus three, and one. Twenty-four minus nine plus two gives seventeen, which lands on six. There is no arithmetic error. Any three submitted values at distinct trustee positions fit a quadratic on our dial, even if a card is false.

Our toy vault has an extra check: it knows the correct opening mark. It rejects six and sounds the alarm. That tells the trustees their answer is wrong, but it does not say who supplied the false card. This alarm comes from the vault, not from secret sharing itself.

Bring in a fourth card. The curve through the first three submitted values predicts that trustee four holds five. But trustee four actually holds two. Those cards cannot all come from the dealer's quadratic. We have detected a disagreement without consulting the vault. Have we identified its source?

No. Suppose each trustee in turn supplied the false card. Fit a curve to the other three. Leaving out trustees one, two, three, and four gives possible secrets eight, three, five, and six. Each row agrees with the other cards. Each explanation is possible from these four cards alone.
Now the fifth trustee arrives with six. Keep the assumption that at most one submitted card is false. Look at our candidate explanations. Could this extra card tell us which trustee supplied the lie?

Yes. Extend each candidate to the fifth position. Only the dealer's curve agrees with four of the five cards. Its secret is five. It predicts one at trustee three, whose submitted card says two. That is the false card. The other candidates fail this extra check.

Why can there be only one such curve? Imagine two different curves each agreeing with four of these five cards. Their sets of matching positions must overlap in at least three positions. Even if each curve misses a different card, only those two positions can be outside the overlap.

At those shared positions, both curves have the value on the same submitted card. They therefore agree at three points. We already proved that two quadratics on this dial which agree at three distinct positions are the same curve. With at most one false card, the honest dealer's curve fits at least four, so it is the unique answer.

More false cards would break that argument. Checking consistency and correcting a lie require extra work and explicit assumptions. Basic secret sharing protects what the cards reveal; it does not authenticate them. In this example, with an honest dealer and at most one false share, the extra cards let us recover the secret and locate the bad card.

Back at the vault, use the genuine cards again. Trustees one, two and three bring eight, three and one. Their recipe gives five at position zero, and the door opens. Now we know why those cards work together.

Trustees four and five still hold two and six. Their observations fit eleven different recipes, one for each possible secret. These are recipes on the dial, shown as dots at the allowed positions. The gold column contains every possible opening mark.

For each proposed secret, exactly one of the hundred and twenty-one spin pairs produces these cards. Fair independent spins make that likelihood the same for every secret. So the cards do not change what the pair knew beforehand, even if some secrets were already more likely.

The method also lets us choose a different rule. Add more trustees, keeping their positions distinct and away from zero. Suppose any four of seven genuine shares should recover the secret. How many secret spins should the dealer use?

Three spins, one fewer than the number of shares needed. Keep the secret as the constant term, then add a times position, b times position squared, and c times position cubed. This is a polynomial of degree at most three. Each spin can still land on zero.

Here is a new dealing on the same dial. The first three trustees hold four, zero and nine. The table lists every recipe that fits those observations. There are eleven columns, one for each secret. Every column has exactly one possible spin triple.

Now trustee four brings three. Extend each candidate recipe to that position. Only the column for secret five predicts the new card correctly. That fourth genuine share removes the ambiguity. The other columns give different predictions, so they cannot explain all the observations.

Any four genuine shares work, not just this group. Subtract two candidate cubics. Unless their difference is zero everywhere, its degree is at most three, so it cannot have four distinct roots on this prime dial. Any three shares, together with any proposed secret, instead specify a unique candidate. Equal spin probabilities give equal likelihoods again.

Shamir calls the secret D, the shares pieces, and the threshold k. His abstract says that even complete knowledge of k minus one pieces reveals absolutely no information about D. The reconstruction method is Lagrange interpolation. Shamir also cites a different scheme by Blakley; that reference is a further reading lead.

Return to our original rule and genuine cards. Any three reconstruct the secret. Any two add no information, not even about whether the secret is odd. That promise depends on the honest dealer and fair, independent, secret spins. It protects what the cards reveal; it does not authenticate them or erase what was already known.
